title: CS161 09: Public-Key Encryption and Digital Signatures

questions.q: Alice wants to send Bob a confidential message using public-key encryption. Which key does she encrypt with?
choices: Her own private key
Her own public key
Bob's public key
Bob's private key
questions.explain: Anyone can encrypt to Bob with his public key. Only Bob's private key can decrypt.

questions.q: Bob shares his private key only with the people who need to send him messages, such as Alice.
questions.explain: Bob tells no one his private key, not even Alice. People sending him messages only need his public key.

questions.q: Which drawback of symmetric-key cryptography is public-key cryptography mainly designed to fix?
choices: Symmetric ciphers cannot provide confidentiality
Symmetric ciphers are much slower than public-key ones
Alice and Bob must somehow coordinate to set up a shared secret key first
Symmetric keys must be published openly
questions.explain: The problem is key management. Symmetric crypto needs a secret shared in advance. Public-key crypto lets strangers communicate without one. Symmetric crypto is actually much faster.

questions.q: Alice picks a random symmetric key K, encrypts K under Bob's public key, and sends Bob the ciphertext. What happens next?
choices: Bob decrypts it with his public key to recover K
Bob decrypts it with his private key to recover K, and then they both use K with a symmetric cipher
Bob has to send K back encrypted under Alice's public key before anyone can use it
K is now public, so it can only be used for integrity
questions.explain: This is how public-key crypto solves key management. It delivers a symmetric key, and the rest of the conversation uses fast symmetric crypto with K.

questions.q: Public-key cryptography is also called ______ cryptography.
questions.explain: It is asymmetric because encryption and decryption use different keys (public and private).

questions.q: Which statement describes a one-way function f?
choices: Given x, f(x) is hard to compute, but given y, an x with f(x) = y is easy to find
Only someone holding a secret key can compute f
Given x, f(x) is easy to compute, but given y, an x with f(x) = y is hard to find
f is easy to compute and to invert, but its outputs look random
questions.explain: One-way means easy to compute forward and hard to invert.

questions.q: How does a trapdoor one-way function differ from an ordinary one-way function?
choices: A secret piece of information (the trapdoor) makes it easy to invert for whoever knows it
Everyone can easily compute it in both directions
It can only be evaluated with the secret key
It never has collisions
questions.explain: It is still easy to compute and hard to invert in general. Someone who knows the backdoor K, though, can easily find x such that f(x) = y.

questions.q: In a public-key scheme built from a trapdoor one-way function, holding the private key makes decryption easy but makes encryption hard.
questions.explain: The private key unlocks the trapdoor, so computing f⁻¹ (decryption) becomes easy. Computing f (encryption) stays easy for everyone.

questions.q: RSA hardness: n = pq for large primes p and q. Given c = m^e mod n and e, finding m is hard. Which extra information makes finding m easy?
choices: The bit length of n
The factorization of n (that is, p or q)
A ciphertext of a different message
The value of e mod 3
questions.explain: The factorization is the trapdoor. Knowing p gives q = n/p, and from there it is easy to recover m.

questions.q: Discrete log setting: p is a large prime and g is a generator. An attacker knows g, p, A = g^a mod p and B = g^b mod p. Which of these would let them easily compute g^(ab) mod p?
choices: The exponent a
The product A × B mod p
The exponent b
The prime p
questions.explain: With a, compute B^a = g^(ab). With b, compute A^b. A × B = g^(a+b), which anyone can compute and which doesn't help. p is already public.

questions.q: Basic (textbook) RSA encryption with no padding is IND-CPA secure.
questions.explain: Basic RSA is deterministic. Encrypting the same message twice gives the same ciphertext, so an eavesdropper can tell when a message repeats.

questions.q: Why does sending the same message twice with basic RSA leak information?
choices: Two encryptions reveal the private key
The modulus n changes between messages
RSA ciphertexts are longer than the plaintext
Encryption is deterministic, so identical plaintexts give identical ciphertexts
questions.explain: Without randomness, an adversary can see that the same message was sent again. That is why RSA adds randomness through a padding mode.

questions.q: Despite the name, RSA padding modes are most similar to which of these?
choices: Padding in block cipher modes
MAC tags
IVs in block cipher modes
A hash function's compression step
questions.explain: RSA padding mixes in randomness so the ciphertext looks random, which is the job an IV does. It is not a deterministic way to extend the message.

questions.q: Name (acronym or full name) a common RSA padding scheme that adds randomness to encryption.
questions.explain: OAEP = Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding.

questions.q: At a high level, what does OAEP do?
choices: Appends a fixed byte pattern until the message reaches the block length
Generates a random key, uses it to scramble the message, and encrypts both the scrambled message and the random key
Hashes the message and encrypts only the hash
Encrypts the message twice under two different public keys
questions.explain: To get the message back, you need both the scrambled message and the random key so you can undo the scrambling. The random key makes each ciphertext different.

questions.q: Like block cipher padding, public-key padding is a deterministic algorithm for extending a message.
questions.explain: Public-key padding is a way to mix in randomness. The ciphertext looks random but still decrypts to the original plaintext.

questions.q: The security of RSA encryption rests on the belief that which task is hard?
choices: Computing m^e mod n
Factoring the large modulus n into its prime factors p and q
Finding a collision in SHA-256
Guessing the public exponent e
questions.explain: Anyone can compute m^e mod n, and e is public. An attacker can't break RSA unless they can factor n.

questions.q: In El Gamal, Bob's private key is b and his public key is B = g^b mod p. How does Alice encrypt a message m?
choices: (g^b mod p, m × r mod p)
(m^B mod p, g^r mod p)
(g^r mod p, m × B^r mod p) for a fresh random r
(B^r mod p, m × g^r mod p) with r = b
questions.explain: The ciphertext is a pair (R, S) with R = g^r mod p and S = m × B^r mod p. Alice picks a new random r in 0…p−2 for each message.

questions.q: Bob receives an El Gamal ciphertext (R, S). How does he decrypt it?
choices: R^b × S mod p
S^(−b) × R mod p
S^b mod p
R^(−b) × S mod p
questions.explain: R^(−b) × S = g^(−rb) × m × g^(br) = m (mod p). The R^(−b) factor cancels the B^r = g^(br) factor in S.

questions.q: Toy El Gamal: p = 23, g = 5, and Bob's private key is b = 6. What is Bob's public key B = g^b mod p?
Same toy setup (p = 23, g = 5, B = 8). Alice encrypts m = 10 with r = 3. What is the second ciphertext component, S = m × B^r mod p?
questions.explain: B^3 = 512 ≡ 6 (mod 23), so S = 10 × 6 = 60 ≡ 14. The first component is R = 5^3 = 125 ≡ 10. Check: Bob gets R^b = 10^6 ≡ 6, whose inverse is 4 (6 × 4 = 24 ≡ 1), and 4 × 14 = 56 ≡ 10 = m.

questions.q: If you view El Gamal as a Diffie-Hellman exchange, Alice and Bob end up sharing a key K. Which value is K?
choices: g^(r+b) mod p
r × b mod p
g^(rb) mod p, which equals both B^r and R^b
B × R mod p
questions.explain: Bob's long-term key is B = g^b, and Alice's fresh one-time key is R = g^r. Alice computes K = B^r and Bob computes K = R^b. Both equal g^(rb).

questions.q: To save effort, Alice can safely reuse the same random r for every El Gamal message she sends to Bob.
questions.explain: A fresh r for each message makes K = B^r new every time, so the key material is used only once. Reusing r reuses K, which is like reusing a one-time pad.

questions.q: The final step of El Gamal, S = m × K mod p, is best described as:
choices: A MAC over m
A one-time pad that uses multiplication mod p instead of XOR
A hash of m
A block cipher in CBC mode
questions.explain: For any ciphertext S and any guessed message m, exactly one K satisfies S = m × K mod p. So, just as with XOR, S alone reveals nothing about m.

questions.q: An attacker intercepts a simplified El Gamal ciphertext (R, S) that encrypts M. Which modified ciphertext will Bob decrypt to 2M?
choices: (2R mod p, S)
(R^2 mod p, S)
(2R mod p, 2S mod p)
(R, 2S mod p)
questions.explain: R^(−b) × 2S = 2 × (R^(−b) × S) = 2M. Changing R instead changes the R^(−b) factor and doesn't give 2M. This malleability is one reason public-key encryption is used only to carry session keys.

questions.q: Why doesn't the plain Diffie-Hellman protocol give public-key encryption by itself?
choices: It needs a trusted third party
Alice and Bob agree on a shared secret, but neither controls its value, so it can't carry a message they choose
It only works with RSA moduli
It sends the shared secret in the clear
questions.explain: In Diffie-Hellman the shared secret comes out random. El Gamal adds one step: Alice multiplies her message by that shared value.

questions.q: The simplified El Gamal scheme shown in the notes is semantically secure without any changes.
questions.explain: For technical reasons, the simplified scheme is not semantically secure. With some tweaks it can be made semantically secure. It is also malleable (M can be turned into 2M).

questions.q: Bob broadcasts his public key. Attila sends a spoofed broadcast that appears to come from Bob but contains a public key Attila generated. If Alice uses that key, what can Attila do?
choices: Nothing, since he doesn't know Bob's private key
Recover Bob's private key
Decrypt the messages Alice meant for Bob, using his own private key
Learn only the lengths of Alice's messages
questions.explain: Alice encrypted under Attila's key, so Attila can intercept the messages and decrypt them with the private key he chose. Broadcasting a key does not protect against active attacks.

questions.q: Alice needs to get Bob's public key over some channel. What must that channel guarantee?
choices: Confidentiality only
Both confidentiality and integrity
Integrity (no one can tamper with the key); confidentiality is not needed
Neither, since public keys are public
questions.explain: The public key doesn't need to stay secret, but Alice must be sure it really is Bob's key and wasn't swapped.

questions.q: Public keys are meant to be public, so simply broadcasting your public key is enough to protect against active attackers.
questions.explain: An active attacker can broadcast a fake key that claims to be yours. Recipients need a channel that protects integrity.

questions.q: Which approach gives authentic public keys without trusting any network channel, but requires meeting in person?
choices: Emailing the key in plaintext
Key-signing parties, or printing your public key on a business card
Posting the key on an unauthenticated web page
Encrypting the key with itself
questions.explain: Swapping keys face to face ensures integrity, but Alice and Bob have to meet in advance.

questions.q: Why do systems usually use public-key cryptography only to send session keys, and then switch to symmetric crypto?
choices: Public-key operations are very slow (e.g., raising a 2048-bit number to a 2048-bit power mod a 2048-bit number)
Public-key encryption cannot provide confidentiality
Some public-key schemes are only safe for random messages (e.g., RSA without OAEP)
Some schemes let an attacker change the message (e.g., turning M into 2M in simplified El Gamal)
Once a public key is published, symmetric keys never need to be exchanged
questions.explain: Public-key crypto is expensive and hard to make IND-CPA secure. Using it only to carry random session keys avoids both problems.

questions.q: A protocol uses a separate key for each direction (Alice→Bob and Bob→Alice), and separate keys for encryption and for the MAC. How many symmetric session keys does it need?
questions.explain: 2 directions × 2 purposes (encryption, MAC) = 4 keys.

questions.q: Alice sends Bob a message encrypted with session keys, plus the session keys encrypted under Bob's public key. What does Bob do?
choices: Decrypts the session keys with his private key, then decrypts the message with the session keys
Decrypts the message with his private key, then checks the session keys
Decrypts the session keys with his public key
Asks Alice to resend the session keys in plaintext
questions.explain: The public-key layer only protects the session keys. The message itself is encrypted symmetrically (e.g., AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA-256).

questions.q: Digital signatures are essentially the public-key version of which symmetric primitive?
choices: Block ciphers
Stream ciphers
MACs
Key derivation functions
questions.explain: Like MACs, signatures provide integrity and authentication, but they use a private signing key and a public verification key.

questions.q: In a digital signature scheme, who can create Bob's signatures, and who can verify them?
choices: Anyone can sign; only Bob can verify
Only Bob can sign and only Bob can verify
Anyone can sign and anyone can verify
Only Bob can sign; anyone with his public key can verify
questions.explain: This is the reverse of encryption. The private key is needed to sign, and the public key is enough to verify.

questions.q: In a signature scheme, the public key is also called the ______ key.
questions.explain: Public key = verification key. Private key = signing key.

questions.q: In a signature scheme, the private key is also called the ______ key.
questions.explain: Private key = signing key. Public key = verification key.

questions.q: Which algorithms make up a digital signature scheme?
choices: Encrypt
KeyGen
Sign
Decrypt
Verify
questions.explain: (PK, SK) = KeyGen(); S = Sign(SK, M); Verify(PK, M, S) returns true or false.

questions.q: KeyGen is a randomized algorithm, and each call produces a new matching keypair.
questions.explain: Each time KeyGen is called, it outputs a fresh (PK, SK) pair.

questions.q: Which statement is the correctness requirement for a signature scheme?
choices: Verify(SK, M, S) = true for any S
If (PK, SK) came from KeyGen and S = Sign(SK, M), then Verify(PK, M, S) = true
Sign(PK, M) = Sign(SK, M)
Verify returns false for every message Bob never signed
questions.explain: Correctness only says that honestly made signatures verify. Rejecting forgeries is a separate requirement, the security property.

questions.q: Why wouldn't it make sense to create signatures with the public key and verify them with the private key?
choices: Verification would be too slow
Anyone could produce a valid signature on a malicious message
The signatures would be too long
It would reveal the private key
questions.explain: If anyone could sign, a signature wouldn't show that the message came from Bob.

questions.q: Euler's totient φ(n) is:
choices: The number of primes less than n
The largest prime factor of n
The number of positive integers less than n that share no common factor with n
n − 1, for every n
questions.explain: φ(n) counts the integers in 1…n−1 that are coprime to n. It equals n − 1 only when n is prime.

questions.q: Euler's theorem says that if gcd(x, n) = 1, then:
choices: x^n ≡ 1 (mod φ(n))
x^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n)
x^φ(n) ≡ 0 (mod n)
x^2 ≡ 1 (mod n)
questions.explain: This is Fact 1. It is the reason raising to the power 3d undoes itself in the RSA proof.

questions.q: p = 5 and q = 11 (both ≡ 2 mod 3), so n = 55. What is φ(n)?
questions.explain: For distinct odd primes, φ(pq) = (p − 1)(q − 1) = 4 × 10 = 40.

questions.q: With φ(n) = 40 (n = 55), find the RSA signing exponent d: the positive value less than 40 with 3d ≡ 1 (mod 40).
Why does this RSA signature construction require p ≡ 2 (mod 3) and q ≡ 2 (mod 3)?
choices: So that n is even
So that p and q are easy to factor
So that φ(pq) = (p − 1)(q − 1) is not a multiple of 3; then some d with 3d ≡ 1 (mod φ(pq)) exists and cube roots are unique
So that H(M) is always less than n
questions.explain: If p ≡ 2 (mod 3), then p − 1 ≡ 1 (mod 3), and the same holds for q. So (p − 1)(q − 1) is not divisible by 3, and 3 has an inverse d mod φ(pq).

questions.q: Let F(x) = x^3 mod n and G(x) = x^d mod n, where 3d ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)). Why is G(F(x)) = x when gcd(x, n) = 1?
choices: Because d = 1/3 as an ordinary fraction
Because 3d = 1 + kφ(n), so x^(3d) = x × (x^φ(n))^k ≡ x × 1^k = x (mod n)
Because cubing mod n is a linear function
Because x^3 ≡ x (mod n) for every x
questions.explain: This is Theorem 1. Write 3d as 1 plus a multiple of φ(n), then apply Euler's theorem.

questions.q: During RSA key generation, which algorithm efficiently computes d from φ(pq) (that is, finds d with 3d ≡ 1 mod φ(pq))?
questions.explain: The extended Euclidean algorithm computes modular inverses. Doing this requires φ(pq), which requires knowing p and q.

questions.q: When p and q are large (e.g., 1024-bit primes), computing cube roots mod n is believed to be infeasible for someone who knows only n (not p, q or d).
questions.explain: It is also believed hard to factor n or to recover d from n. RSA's security depends on this assumption.

questions.q: In the RSA signature scheme described here, what are the public key and the private key?
choices: Public: d; private: n
Public: n = pq; private: d
Public: p; private: q
Public: the hash function H; private: n
questions.explain: Anyone with n can cube mod n to verify. The private d lets the signer take cube roots.

questions.q: How is the RSA signature on a message M computed?
choices: S = M^3 mod n
S = H(M)^3 mod n
S = H(M^d) mod n
S = H(M)^d mod n
questions.explain: Sign_d(M) = H(M)^d mod n, that is, the cube root of H(M) mod n, computed using the trapdoor d.

questions.q: How does a verifier check a signature S on message M under public key n?
choices: Check that S = H(M)^3 mod n
Check that H(M) = S^3 mod n
Check that M = S^d mod n
Check that H(S) = M^3 mod n
questions.explain: A valid signature satisfies H(M) = F(S) = S^3 mod n. Only public values are needed to check this.

questions.q: Public key n = 55, private key d = 27. A message has H(M) = 2. What is its RSA signature S = H(M)^d mod n?
Under public key n = 55, S = 17 is a valid RSA signature on a message with H(M) = 2.
questions.explain: 17^3 = 4913 ≡ 18 (mod 55), since 55 × 89 = 4895. That is not H(M) = 2, so verification fails.

questions.q: A forger without d picks a candidate signature S and computes y = S^3 mod n. Why can't she turn this into a forgery?
choices: Computing S^3 mod n requires d
She would need a message M with H(M) = y, and H is one-way
y is always larger than n
Verification also checks that S was produced recently
questions.explain: Starting from the signature side gets stuck at inverting H, which has no trapdoor.

questions.q: A forger without d picks a message M and computes H(M). What stops her from producing a valid signature?
choices: She can't compute H(M), because H is secret
She needs Bob's public key, which is secret
She can't compute the cube root H(M)^d mod n without the trapdoor
H(M) is always 0 mod n
questions.explain: Starting from the message side gets stuck at inverting F (taking cube roots mod n), which requires the private key.

questions.q: The hash function H in RSA signatures is a trapdoor function, and its trapdoor is part of the signer's private key.
questions.explain: H is a public, standardized one-way function with no trapdoor. Everyone can compute it, and no one can invert it. The only trapdoor is the one for F, namely d.

questions.q: What is the intuition behind the RSA trapdoor used for signatures?
choices: Anyone can take cube roots mod n, but cubing mod n is hard
Multiplying primes is hard, but factoring is easy
Anyone can cube a number mod n, but taking cube roots mod n is believed hard without knowing the factorization of n
Hashing is easy, but checking a hash is hard
questions.explain: F(x) = x^3 mod n is easy for everyone. G(y) = y^d mod n (the cube root) needs d, which comes from the factorization.

questions.q: In the signature security game, when does the adversary Georgia win?
choices: When she outputs any (M, S) for which Verify returns true
When she recovers the private key
When she gets the referee to sign a message of her choice
When she outputs (M, S) for which Verify returns true and M was never one of her signing queries
questions.explain: A forgery only counts if it is on a message the referee was never asked to sign.

questions.q: If Georgia asks the referee to sign M, receives S, and then outputs that same (M, S), she wins the game.
questions.explain: Repeating a signature she was given is not a forgery. M must be a message she never queried.

questions.q: Under the security definition, when is a signature scheme declared insecure?
choices: When Georgia has a strategy to forge with non-negligible probability (say ≥ 1/2^40), given generous computation (say 2^80 steps) and a reasonable number of signing queries (say 2^40)
Only when Georgia can forge, with probability 1, a signature on a specific message the referee chooses
When Georgia can verify signatures without the private key
Only when Georgia learns the private key
questions.explain: Any noticeable chance of forging any new message breaks the scheme. Verifying without the private key is how signatures are supposed to work.

questions.q: Why is this security definition considered very stringent?
choices: It requires signatures to also keep messages confidential
The scheme counts as broken if Georgia forges a signature on any message of her choice, even after getting many messages of her choice signed
The scheme counts as broken if verification ever takes more than 2^40 steps
It hides the public key from Georgia
questions.explain: Georgia gets to pick which messages are signed and which message to forge on. The scheme must resist all of that. RSA signatures are believed to meet this definition.

questions.q: Besides the public-key math, what else does signature security depend on?
choices: The secrecy of the verification key
The length of the message
The underlying hash function; signatures have been broken in the past through hash collisions
How fast the verifier is
questions.explain: The scheme signs H(M). If H is compromised, signatures can be broken even when the public-key algorithm is fine.

questions.q: An attacker finds two messages M1 ≠ M2 with H(M1) = H(M2), and gets Bob to sign the harmless M1. What can she do?
choices: Nothing, because the signature is tied to M1 only
Recover Bob's private key d
Present Bob's signature on M1 as a valid signature on M2
Sign arbitrary new messages
questions.explain: Verification only checks H(M) = S^3 mod n. Because H(M2) = H(M1), the same S verifies for M2.

questions.q: Modern digital signature schemes, such as RSA signatures, are believed to meet this stringent security definition.
questions.explain: They are believed secure as long as the underlying hash function also holds up.
